power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Digital tools make diagnostic tests easy to build, but convenience does not guarantee that scores reflect the intended thinking processes.

This study examined item quality and reliability of Draft 1 of the Statistical Reasoning Diagnostic Assessment for Psychology Students (SRDA-PSY), an online two-tier diagnostic test covering six domains of statistical reasoning, interpreting the results through cognitive psychology principles.
Forty-one psychology students took the test via Google Forms.
Classical test theory analyses (difficulty, discrimination, distractor effectiveness, two-tier response patterns, and KR-20) were triangulated with a single expert review.
The mean score was 83%, and 26 of 41 items were very easy.
All 15 items of moderate or easy difficulty discriminated well, but only 21% of distractors were functional.

The key was the longest option in 57 of 63 option sets, and the six items without this cue were much harder (mean p = .53 vs. .89), suggesting that many items could be answered with an option-form heuristic rather than analytic reasoning.
On twotier items, students often endorsed a correct general principle but failed to apply it to the case, consistent with the view that intuitive and scientific conceptions can coexist.
KR-20 was .90 but dropped to .78 when the two lowest-scoring respondents were removed, and expert review and empirical data detected different weaknesses.
The content of SRDA-PSY is promising, but option form must be revised so that scores reflect statistical reasoning.
Digital assessment development, including AI-assisted item writing, should combine expert review, empirical tryouts, and automated audits of option-form cues.
Educational technology has changed how assessments are built and delivered.
Online forms, digital item banks, and large language models allow instructors to write, distribute, and score many items in a short time (Kasneci et al., 2023; Swiecki et al., 2022).

text.text: Artificial intelligence systems can already generate multiple-choice items judged comparable in quality to humanwritten items (Cheung et al., 2023; Kurdi et al., 2020).

text.text: This convenience carries an old question from psychological measurement into a new context: do the responses recorded by a digital system actually reflect the thinking processes the test is meant to measure?
The question matters for diagnostic assessment because its scores are used as feedback, and feedback supports learning only when the information it carries is accurate (Wisniewski et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The question matters for diagnostic assessment because its scores are used as feedback, and feedback supports learning only when the information it carries is accurate <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Wisniewski et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Statistics is a domain that needs such assessment.
Psychology students can run a t test correctly yet still misinterpret p values, draw causal conclusions from correlational data, or generalize results beyond the sample.

Misinterpretations of p values and confidence intervals are widespread among psychology students and researchers as well as researchers in other fields (Kalinowski et al., 2018; X.-K. Lyu et al., 2020; Z. Lyu et al., 2018), prompting statisticians to call for inference that no longer rests on the "p < .05" threshold (Wasserstein et al., 2019).

Lyu et al., 2018)</ref>, prompting statisticians to call for inference that no longer rests on the "p < .05" threshold <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Wasserstein et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: When software and artificial intelligence can produce output and interpretation within seconds, the competence increasingly needed is the ability to judge whether that output is appropriate.
Assessments that focus on computation cannot reveal this ability.
Existing statistical reasoning instruments such as REALI (Sabbag et al., 2018) measure literacy and reasoning in general but were not designed to map misconceptions in psychology-specific cases.
text.formatted: Existing statistical reasoning instruments such as REALI <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Sabbag et al., 2018)</ref> measure literacy and reasoning in general but were not designed to map misconceptions in psychology-specific cases.

text.text: Three principles of cognitive psychology are relevant to judging whether a digital diagnostic assessment works as intended.

First, dual-process theory holds that answers can be produced by fast intuitive processes or by slower analytic processes, and a correct answer does not necessarily indicate that analytic processing took place (De Neys, 2023).
Multiple-choice items offer surface cues such as the length and tone of the options.
When the key can be recognized from these cues, the item can be answered heuristically.
An experiment on items whose key was longer than the other options showed that this kind of item-writing flaw tends to make items easier (Casu & García-García, 2018).
text.formatted: An experiment on items whose key was longer than the other options showed that this kind of item-writing flaw tends to make items easier <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Casu & García-García, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, conceptual change research shows that misconceptions do not simply disappear after instruction but can coexist with scientific concepts (Vosniadou, 2019).
text.formatted: Second, conceptual change research shows that misconceptions do not simply disappear after instruction but can coexist with scientific concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Vosniadou, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The Statistical Reasoning Diagnostic Assessment for Psychology Students (SRDA-PSY) was developed as an online diagnostic assessment of statistical reasoning for psychology students.

It covers six domains: (1) data and variable reasoning, (2) choosing analyses, (3) variability, sampling, and generalization, (4) statistical inference, (5) interpreting effects and relationships, and (6) critical statistical judgment, including evaluation of interpretations produced by software and artificial intelligence.
All items are based on psychology cases, and most use a two-tier format.
Expert review can judge content appropriateness but cannot establish how students respond to the items, so an empirical tryout is needed before the instrument is used for diagnosis.
At an early stage with a small sample, classical test theory item analysis is more appropriate than item response models that require large samples.
This study examined item quality and reliability of Draft 1 of SRDA-PSY and interpreted the findings through principles of cognitive psychology in the context of technology-based assessment.
Specifically, it addressed four questions: (1) What are the difficulty and discrimination of the items?
(2) How effective are the distractors, and what response patterns appear on two-tier items?
(3) How reliable are the total and domain scores?
(4) How do the empirical findings compare with expert review of item content?
This study was the initial tryout stage of instrument development, using a quantitative psychometric design based on classical test theory complemented by expert review.
Participants were undergraduate psychology students at one faculty of psychology in a public university in North Sumatra, Indonesia.
Forty-two responses were collected from two classes: Quantitative Research for Behavioral Sciences (2025 cohort, third semester) and Statistics for Behavioral Sciences (2026 cohort, first semester).
One student submitted twice, so only the first submission was analyzed.
The final sample comprised 41 students, 17 from the 2025 cohort and 24 from the 2026 cohort.
Draft 1 of SRDA-PSY contains 45 items written from a six-domain blueprint: D1 (6 items), D2 (8), D3 (7), D4 (8), D5 (8), and D6 (8).
Items were designed at three cognitive levels: Interpret (10 items), Reason (20 items), and Evaluate (15 items).
Twenty-two items use a two-tier format, 19 are single-tier multiple-choice items, and 4 are short constructed-response items.

Each multiple-choice item has four options, and each distractor was written to represent a specific misconception, such as interpreting a p value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true or equating a large sample with a representative one.
Items were administered in Indonesian.
The instrument was administered via Google Forms on October 24 and 25, 2026.
Students were asked to work independently without statistical software, the internet, help from peers, or artificial intelligence.
Students who completed all items received five bonus points toward their final course grade based on completion, not accuracy.
Students were informed that their responses would be used for instrument development.
One expert reviewer rated each item holistically on a scale from 1 to 4 (4 = strong,3 = minor revision,2 = substantial revision,1 = not aligned with the construct) and provided qualitative comments.
Single-tier multiple-choice items were scored 1 if correct and 0 otherwise.
Two-tier items were scored 1 only when both the first-tier answer and the second-tier reason were correct.
The four constructed-response items had not yet been scored, so analyses were based on 41 dichotomous items.
The difficulty index (p) was classified as hard (< .30), moderate (.30 to .69), easy (.70 to .89), or very easy (≥ .90).

text.text: Items that met the empirical criteria but received a rating of 2 from the expert were moved to content revision.

A rater-agreement content validity coefficient was not computed because only one rater was available, so the expert review was treated as qualitative evidence and triangulated with the empirical results.
All analyses were conducted in Python (pandas, NumPy, and SciPy).
Total scores on the 41 dichotomous items ranged from 14 to 41, with a mean of 34.22 (SD = 5.93; median = 35).
The distribution was strongly negatively skewed (skewness = -1.73), and five respondents answered every item correctly.

The mean score of the 2025 cohort (M = 34.88, SD = 5.95) was nearly identical to that of the 2026 cohort (M = 33.75, SD = 5.99), even though the 2025 cohort had one more year of statistics instruction.
The mean difficulty index was .83.
Twenty-six items were very easy, 6 easy, 9 moderate, and none hard.
Four items were answered correctly by all respondents (D4-05, D5-02, D6-01, and D6-08).
Table 1 shows that items became easier from D1 and D2 toward D5 and D6.

text.text: The order of difficulty by cognitive level was the reverse of the design.
Evaluate items, designed to be the most demanding, were the easiest (mean p = .94), followed by Interpret (.86) and Reason (.76).
From a dual-process perspective, this inversion indicates that the Evaluate items did not yet require analytic processing.
These items ask students to judge a claim, and the key was almost always a cautious rejection of an overstated claim.
Students familiar with multiple-choice tests can rely on the simple intuition that the most cautious answer is usually correct.
De Neys (2023) emphasizes that intuitive responses can yield correct answers without analytic deliberation.

The consequence for diagnostic assessment is clear: items that do not create conflict between the intuitive answer and the reasoned answer cannot distinguish students who actually reason from students who merely recognize a pattern.
The similar scores of first-and third-semester students support this interpretation, because a test sensitive to reasoning should capture a year of learning in statistics.
By rit, 23 items were very good, 6 good, 6 fair, 2 poor (D1-03 and D4-04), and 4 could not be computed because they had no score variance.
By the D index, only 16 items were good or very good, whereas 21 were poor.
Table 2 shows that this discrepancy is closely tied to difficulty.

text.text: On very easy items, rit could be high (e.g., D6-02, rit = .75, p = .95) because the one or two errors that occurred came from the lowest-scoring respondents.
The strongest discrimination was found for D2-03 (p = .39; rit = .54; D = .91), D1-04 (rit = .50; D = .73), and D1-05 (rit = .49; D = .73).
These findings show that SRDA-PSY content can differentiate students when items are of adequate difficulty.

In measurement terms, information about differences in ability comes mostly from items whose difficulty matches respondents' ability; items answered correctly by almost everyone are informative only about a handful of the lowest scorers.
In the context of educational technology, this finding is also relevant for instructors who read automatic item statistics from online quiz platforms.

Item-total correlations in small samples are highly sensitive to one or two respondents, so revision decisions should not rest on a single index. Rezigalla et al. (2024) likewise found that distractor quality is related to difficulty and discrimination, so the three parameters should be read together.

A total of 148 distractors were chosen by fewer than 5% of respondents, and one distractor was chosen by five respondents but equally often by the upper and lower groups.
Twenty-five items had no functional distractor, and only D1-05 reached DE ≥ .80.

text.text: Examination of option form revealed a systematic pattern.
The key was the longest option in 57 of 63 option sets (90%), including all 22 second-tier option sets.
Keys averaged 134 characters, about twice the mean length of distractors (63 characters).
Absolute words such as "certainly," "always," "only," or "must" appeared in 36% of distractors but in only 13% of keys.
The six items whose key was not the longest option (D1-02, D2-01, D2-02, D2-03, D3-04, and D4-04) had a mean p of .53, far below the mean of the other 35 items (p = .89).
Figure 1 shows that these six items (triangles) fall in the moderate-to-easy range and all have D ≥ .54.

text.text: A diagnostic distractor works only if it is phrased the way students themselves think about the concept.
The SRDA-PSY distractors were written from documented misconceptions, but many were phrased as short, absolute statements.

Such statements are easy to reject with a simple heuristic of avoiding extreme answers, so the distractors never competed with the key. Casu and García-García (2018) found that items whose key is longer than the other options tend to be easier, and Breakall et al. (2019) reported that implausible distractors were the most frequent item-writing flaw in more than a thousand instructor-written multiple-choice exam items. Gierl et al. (2017) likewise stress that implausible distractors reduce the diagnostic information of an item.

text.text: Educational technology offers concrete remedies.

Students' constructed responses in this tryout contain misconceptions in their own words, such as causal claims from correlational data and generalization to all Indonesian students from a single-university sample. Ali et al. (2016) found that replacing nonfunctional distractors with errors drawn from students' open-ended answers improved score reliability, and Shin et al. (2019) showed that students' written responses can be processed with topic modeling to generate distractors.

text.text: Equalizing option length should also take cognitive load theory into account.

It is better done by condensing the key than by lengthening the distractors, because long text adds extraneous cognitive load, especially when the test is taken on a mobile phone screen (Sweller et al., 2019).

text.text: Across the 22 two-tier items, the mean false positive rate was 5% and the mean false negative rate was 12%.
False negatives exceeded 10% on nine items (D1-01, D1-04, D1-05, D1-06, D2-01, D2-02, D2-03, D3-02, and D4-04), and false positives exceeded 10% on three items (D2-01, D2-03, and D2-05).
The most striking case was D4-04, which asked respondents to compare the precision of two studies based on the width of their confidence intervals.
Twentyfive respondents (61%) chose the distractor "Study P is more precise because its interval is wider, so it is more certain to contain the true value" (translated from Indonesian).
This distractor was chosen more often by the lower group (8 students) than by the upper group (3 students).
Yet 24 of the 25 students who chose it selected the correct second-tier reason, namely that a narrower interval indicates a more precise estimate.
High false negative rates indicate that second-tier reasons can be recognized as true general statements without being linked to the first-tier answer.
The D4-04 case reveals a more interesting psychological phenomenon.
Students endorsed the principle that a narrower interval means a more precise estimate, yet in the concrete case they chose the wider interval because it felt safer.
This pattern fits Vosniadou's (2019) view that a scientific concept can be stored as declarative knowledge while an intuitive conception continues to guide application.

text.text: In dualprocess terms, students did not detect the conflict between the intuition that "wider is more certain" and the principle they themselves endorsed (De Neys, 2023).

text.text: This misconception is therefore worth keeping as a diagnostic target.
What needs to be fixed is the link between the two tiers.
Branching features in online forms allow the reasons displayed to depend on the first-tier answer, so that a reason cannot be chosen independently of the answer.
KR-20 for the 37 items with score variance was .90 (95% CI [.84, .94]; SEM = 1.92).
The sensitivity analysis in Table 4 shows that this coefficient was strongly influenced by the two lowest-scoring respondents, whereas deleting any single item raised KR-20 by at most .003.

text.text: Domain-level reliability ranged from .55 to .84 (D1 = .55, D2 = .70, D3 = .59, D4 = .58, D5 = .73, D6 = .84).
The highest KR-20, for D6, should be read with caution because all D6 items had p ≥ .93.
A coefficient of .90 cannot be taken as evidence that SRDA-PSY is reliable, because totalscore variance was largely carried by the difference between two respondents and everyone else.
The available data cannot establish whether the low scores of these two respondents reflect low ability or low effort.

In an unproctored low-stakes online test with an incentive based on completion, some respondents may answer quickly without reading the items. Wise (2017) shows that such rapid-guessing behavior can be identified from item response times and should be controlled for scores to be interpretable.

text.text: Ten items were retained, four of them without changes, whereas 29 items were revised and 6 were rewritten.
No D6 item met the criteria for retention.
The two sources of evidence detected different weaknesses because they work differently.
The reviewer read the items one at a time with the key in view, so option-form cues that are systematic across items were hard to notice.
Item statistics, on the other hand, cannot detect a conceptual error in the key as long as more able respondents still choose it, as with D1-04.

This finding is consistent with the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, which call for validity evidence from multiple sources, including test content and response processes (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014).

text.text: The implication becomes more important when item writing is assisted by artificial intelligence.

Large language models can produce many items quickly (Cheung et al., 2023; Kasneci et al., 2023), so the number of items can grow faster than the capacity for expert review. Swiecki et al. (2022) argue that artificial intelligence should prompt a redesign of assessment rather than simply speed up old practices.

text.text: For SRDA-PSY and similar digital assessments, the item development pipeline should combine expert review, empirical tryouts, and automated cross-item audits of option length, key position, and the frequency of absolute words.
Such audits are cheap to compute and can catch cues that item-by-item reading misses.
This study has several limitations.
The small sample (n = 41) meant that the upper and lower groups contained only 11 students each, so a single response could shift the D index by .09.
Respondents came from one faculty, and testing was unproctored and online, so response effort could not be verified.
The four constructed-response items have not yet been analyzed, and expert review came from a single reviewer using holistic ratings, so quantitative content validity evidence is not yet available.
The psychological interpretations offered here, particularly regarding the use of option-form heuristics, remain inferential and should be tested with response process data.
Draft 1 of SRDA-PSY is not yet ready for use as a diagnostic assessment, but its content provides a promising foundation.
Items of moderate and easy difficulty discriminated well, whereas 26 of 41 items were too easy and 79% of distractors were nonfunctional.
This ease stemmed mainly from keys that could be recognized by their form, so many items could be answered heuristically without statistical reasoning.
Two-tier response patterns showed that students can endorse a correct statistical principle while still applying a mistaken intuitive conception.
Total-score reliability appeared high but depended on the two lowest-scoring respondents, and domain-level reliability was insufficient for diagnostic feedback.
Of the 45 items, 10 were retained, 29 revised, and 6 rewritten.

Revisions for Draft 2 should prioritize equalizing the length and tone of keys and distractors by condensing the keys, replacing distractors with misconceptions drawn from students' constructed responses, and linking second-tier options to first-tier choices through the branching features of online forms.

The next tryout should involve a larger and more diverse sample, a panel of several experts, a platform that records item-level response times, and thinkaloud interviews to test whether correct answers are indeed supported by sound reasoning.

For developers of digital assessment more broadly, these findings show that the ease with which technology lets us write and deliver items must be matched by an understanding of how students process those items.
